facts.raw_span: A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use
altered mental status
febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10)
left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5)
leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL)
Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates
Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage
Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema
Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³
no valvular vegetations
Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³
Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement

concepts.why: The patient has altered mental status, fever, and CSF findings consistent with meningoencephalitis, including elevated WBCs and protein.
The patient has imaging findings consistent with cerebral vasculitis, including a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity.
The patient has a history of intravenous heroin use and urine toxicology positive for benzodiazepines and opiates, which could contribute to toxic leukoencephalopathy.
The patient has imaging findings consistent with a brain abscess, including a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia and CSF findings consistent with infection.
The patient has imaging findings consistent with stroke, including a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia and left upper- and lower-limb weakness.
The patient has altered mental status and a history of intravenous heroin use, which could contribute to metabolic encephalopathy.

rationales.F01: Hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use may contribute to various neurological conditions, but the connection is not specific enough to rule in or out any of the listed concepts.
rationales.F02: Altered mental status is a nonspecific finding that could be associated with several of the listed concepts, including Subacute Meningoencephalitis, Toxic Leukoencephalopathy, Brain Abscess, and Metabolic Encephalopathy.
rationales.F06: The presence of benzodiazepines and opiates in urine toxicology could suggest Toxic Leukoencephalopathy or Metabolic Encephalopathy, but the connection is not strong enough to rule in these conditions decisively.
rationales.F07: The hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect on head CT could be indicative of several conditions, including Brain Abscess, Stroke, or Subacute Meningoencephalitis.
rationales.F09: The findings from the lumbar puncture, including the elevated opening pressure and the presence of WBCs in the CSF, strongly suggest Subacute Meningoencephalitis or Brain Abscess.
rationales.F11: The progression of CSF findings, including the increased WBC count and decreased glucose level, further supports the diagnosis of Subacute Meningoencephalitis or Brain Abscess.
rationales.F12: The progression of MRI findings, including the new involvement of the left basal ganglia and the development of necrosis, supports the diagnosis of Subacute Meningoencephalitis, Brain Abscess, or possibly Cerebral Vasculitis.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation with febrile and altered mental status, along with CSF findings of elevated WBCs, protein, and decreased glucose, strongly supports Subacute Meningoencephalitis. The progression of symptoms and imaging findings despite empirical treatment also aligns with this diagnosis.
